title: More Than 500 Rohingya Feared Dead After Two Boats Vanish Off Myanmar. The World's Deadliest Sea Route Keeps Claiming Lives.
excerpt: One boat carrying 250 people lost contact in late June. A second with 280 aboard is believed to have sunk on July 8. The UN calls them the world's riskiest maritime crossings.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over 500 Rohingya are feared dead after two boats sank off Myanmar's coast.
  • The Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal are the world's deadliest maritime routes for refugees.
  • 860 of 6,500 Rohingya attempting the crossing were reported missing or dead last year.
  • Rohingya face decades of persecution and dire conditions in refugee camps.
  • UN calls for stronger regional efforts to prevent further deaths at sea.

An estimated 500 people, most of them members of Myanmar's persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority, are feared dead after two overcrowded boats sank within days of each other off the coast of the war-torn country, the United Nations said Thursday. ## What Happened The International Organization for Migration and UNHCR issued a joint statement saying both vessels had departed from Myanmar's Rakhine State in late June, carrying mostly Rohingya passengers. The first boat, believed to have carried around 250 people, lost contact shortly after setting off. A second vessel, with an estimated 280 people on board, is believed to have capsized off Myanmar's Ayeyarwady coast on July 8. "While the incidents and casualty figures have yet to be officially confirmed, UNHCR and IOM are gravely concerned by the potentially devastating loss of life," the agencies said. Some of those on board had travelled from Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh, home to the world's largest refugee camp, where more than one million Rohingya live in increasingly dire conditions. ## The Deadliest Sea Route The journey across the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal toward Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand has become the deadliest maritime crossing per capita anywhere in the world. Last year, 860 of the 6,500 Rohingya refugees who attempted the crossing were reported missing or dead — the highest mortality rate of any major migrant sea route globally, worse even than the Mediterranean, according to UNHCR data. The boats set sail outside the regular sailing season, when maritime conditions are typically more hazardous. Recent heavy rainfall and flooding across the region, including deadly mudslides in Cox's Bazar that killed more than a dozen people last week, have made the crossings even more perilous. Nearly 300 people had already been reported missing or dead in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal so far this year, even before this latest disaster. ## Why They Flee

The Rohingya have faced decades of persecution in Myanmar. Denied citizenship under a 1982 law, they have been stripped of access to education, healthcare, employment, and freedom of movement. More than 700,000 fled to Bangladesh in 2017 amid a military-led campaign of murder, rape, and arson that the United States considers a genocide. Myanmar has denied that its actions amount to genocide. Many thousands have followed since, especially as fighting in Rakhine State intensified after Myanmar's 2021 military coup. In the camps, refugees are not allowed to work and face diminishing international aid. With no safe route back to Myanmar and few prospects in Bangladesh, many risk everything on flimsy wooden boats crammed well over capacity. ## A Regional Crisis The UN agencies called for stronger regional and international efforts to prevent further deaths "along one of the world's deadliest maritime routes," including enhanced search-and-rescue capabilities, access to asylum and protection, and stricter action against the smuggling and trafficking networks that organise these voyages. "These reports underscore the devastating impact of protracted conflict and displacement, as well as the continued lack of sustainable solutions for Rohingya communities," the joint statement said.
Rohingya Crisis Overview
›700,000 fled to Bangladesh in 2017.
›Denied citizenship and basic rights in Myanmar.
›Ongoing conflict since Myanmar's 2021 military coup.
›Refugees face diminishing international aid.
For the large Rohingya diaspora communities in Malaysia, Thailand, and across South and Southeast Asia — as well as the broader South Asian diaspora that shares cultural and geographic ties to the region — the tragedy is a reminder that one of the world's longest-running refugee crises continues to claim lives far from the headlines. *Sources: Reuters, The Wall Street Journal, CNN, UN News*
